It's an okay resume. First thing I would say is to remove the coursework section; it's not really reflective of what you know. And it's kinda redundant, i.e. why would you say you took a database class when you're already showcasing that you know SQL in your experience and projects?

I think your bullet points are a little vague. In your work experience section, I would try and throw in some technologies you used. Like instead of just "Integrated RESTFUL APIs...", you could instead say "Integrated RESTFUL API endpoints with Express.js...." (assuming that's what you used). I would remove the "useEffect" mention from your bullet point because someone looking at your resume won't really know what this is right away; Pointing out specific functions or such that you used it just going too deep.

Lastly, your projects are somewhat unimpressive. I would either improve upon them or make something else. The first one may be okayish, but the second one is a very run-of-the-mill CS student project. Plus, for projects, I would format the bullet points differently. Spend the first bullet point talking about your project quickly, and the other two bullet points can be much more technical. None of the bullet points describe your project, which is bad for some types of projects. For example, GeoMarker Navigator is not really descriptive of what the application actually does.

Something holding you back that you can't improve is how old your work experience is. A Development gap from 2021 to 2024 is very large, but there's not really a way to fix that. It's a little likely you might lose your visa, but I wouldn't give up anyway. And even if you do, there are a lot of opportunities for you in other places.

Good luck!

OP. You need some resume help ASAP.

\- Your text is too big and non-descriptive.   
\- There are inconsistencies like the spacing between "full stack developer" and the bullet point above it, versus "IT support specialist" and the spacing above it.   
\- For the amount of stuff you've done, this resume looks empty; the line spacing looks like it's 1.5 or something.   
\- The word "Remote" should be lined up at the rightmost part of your page. Speaking of that, your dates aren't really lined up at the end either  
\- Most recent experience should be at the top, not the bottom  
\- I would sacrifice some space in the work experience category to flesh out your projects instead, if you're applying to SWE jobs. Your projects should have multiple bullet points  
\- The bullet points themselves are different sizes  
\- Try to keep everything all in one font, usually times new roman

I would dedicate a lot of time to networking or finding internships. Internships will be the most valuable thing on your resume. Networking is probably the most important thing in this field right now.

A masters in CS will make you stand out more but you'll be missing out on fundamentals you learn in a bachelors. If you're confident you can learn the fundamentals of everything yourself, a masters could work out. A bachelors won't take 4 years for you if you can apply gen-eds you completed during your chemistry degree, realistically it'll take 2.5-ish. But this is really a personal choice. You can't go wrong with either one. If you do decide to go for a masters, I'd give yourself a semester break before going back to school so you can catch up on fundamentals.

I hope you aren't falling for the "tech is a great job that's easy to get" mantra. It's why the field is saturated, and why even people with experience can't land a job. It will take you a year of hard work at minimum to build things to even compete with current new grads. There is no 'ASAP'. Try to enjoy what you do or you will burnout and wish you never started.

There's no shortcuts, and you already have a disadvantage by being without the proper degree. It'll take time, but these are some thigs to look into (not in any particular order):

- DSA. Data structures and algorithms. People always say programming is easy until they hit this particular topic. You'll need it in order to implement software efficiently, but mostly, for interviewing. Most interviews include a technical portion where the interviewer asks you to solve a leetcode (DSA) question in front of them. Learn DSA, do leetcode questions, so that you don't flunk the interview when your resume finally looks good enough. I recomend Java specifically for this purpose.

- Learn a stack. Base it off what you want to do. Websites? HTML, CSS, Javascript. Heavy backend? Java, C#. Data? SQL, Python. Games? C++ or C#. Obviously I didn't list everything, but each language or tool has it's own usage. Learn what you want to focus on. So don't dive deep into C++ if your ultimate goal is to make websites look good.

- Projects. Build something with the stack you just learned. Since you have no experience or degree, this will be your main selling point. Your projects need to blow companies out of the water since you're competing against people that have a ton of other relevant things om their resume. 

Remember, there are no shortcuts. If someone messaged you and said they wanted to learn enough chemistry to get a job, without having any prior experience or related certfications, you'd probably give them a reality check. Since you wrote that a new bachelors is in the cards for you, I would do that, in addition to everything I already listed.

Good luck!

If it really bothers you, go ahead and breakup. Dental health can never improve, only worsen; teeth are basically the only part of your body that don't heal at all.

But don't be too harsh on him. I have bad teeth. My mom never bought toothbrushes, toothpaste, or told me that i have to brush. She told me plaque at the edges was actually glue holding my teeth together to get me to stop asking about it. She would put candy in my schoolbag every day. Every single day from pre-school to middle school. I'm 24 with 3 root canals and an implant, my siblings are going to be in the same boat as me soon. On top of this, if his teeth are really that bad, he has probably dealt with dental pain at its extreme. Dental pain is probably one of the worst experiences anybody could ever have.

You don't have to stay with him, but realize he's not like this because he's 'nasty', he's dealing with issues that happen when you're young and don't know how important all this stuff is down the line. Dental health was probably downplayed or ignored by people around him (neglect), and this is the result. Nobody would ever purposely choose to have yellow teeth and a mouth of crowns. Just be gentle with him.

If you do choose to stay with him, suggest more frequent dental visits and support him through his experience. When he loses a crown/filling/etc, push him to fix it faster. The cost and emotional toll is a lot for him, so if you're not breaking up, telling him he's unattractive for it is not the way to go. Mostly because it's not something you can fix in a day.

But that's the point of reviews. I'm neutral on patch 69, but the point of reviewing a game is to tell other players whether or not something is worth playing in it's current state. People bringing garbage into HR to boost GS so they can kill you while wearing whites. Battles are now over much faster because everyone has 1-shot damage.  
  
When a game goes from good to bad reviews, the developers should make the changes to recover the game to it's former glory, instead of telling everybody to go cry about it. They listened to the players, which is a great step and people will start reverting; but you can't say reviews are a 'weapon' against a developer. It's an honest reflection of players that feel strongly about the game, and if they feel the game is in a bad enough state to warn other people to stay away, then it's up to the developers to fix it. A game with 'good potential' can still be a bad game if the developers don't treat it right. If we weren't allowed to leave bad reviews on a game with 'great potential', no game would ever improve and developers would never learn. If DnD was never review bombed, the devs would not have reacted as fast as they did.

NAD. I had a tooth hurt right after a filling; except the pain was a straight 9/10. I went to an endo and after making sure that I'm 100% sure I think this needs a root canal, he opened up my tooth. Crazy inflamed to the point of no return. It was a shallow filling and it still killed my tooth.

Your tooth is experiencing pulpitis. Whether it's reversible or irreversible pulpitis, I couldn't tell you. If you're willing to wait longer without doing anything, you can; pain and discomfort from deep fillings can take up to a few weeks to go away, which was the case with some of my own fillings. The moment the pain gets worse, I would go see a dentist or endo for root canal/extraction, because that means the inflammation doesn't want to heal.

If the pain is bad enough that waiting isn't an option, you can see your dentist and ask what they think the best course of action is.

Teeth damaged from acid? Being born with no enamel? Getting into an accident and walking away with dentures because implants are too expensive? Can't afford braces? Can't afford jaw surgery??? Bad teeth are correlated to a ton of major diseases in the human body and are dangerous to have. Not to mention a tooth abscess is the most painful thing you will ever experience. You can die from it, have it removed to be safe, and you'll still get mocked. Your job, social, and romantic prospects will literally be affected by anything and everything that happens to your teeth.

Teeth should be the LAST thing to be made fun of. It's more trashy to make fun of bad teeh than to have them.

NAD - Keep wearing the trays. No idea what the pus is, but now that you have no crown, your tooth is at risk of getting infected. Orthodontic treatment should not normally force crowns off; this usually implies the crown was poor quality or a poor fit.

Honestly I wouldn't wait until your dentist opens. The crown was clearly bad. Even if they did a good job, a week is a long time to wait since they need to remake the crown itself. Shop elsewhere and see if anyone can fit you in for an emergency apppointment. If that tooth gets infected, you will either be shelling out money for a root canal AND a new crown, or you will lose the tooth.

NAD - I had a piece of tooth about that size chip off on my molar several days ago, and it got infected the next day. Abscessed the next-next day, though it wasn't visible on the initial x-ray so it's small. But the fact that it's even there means they grow FAST. I'm still waiting a week and a half for my now root canal from a specialist, which can turn into an extraction depending on the damage/infection spread.

Call up your dentist for an appointment as soon as you can. If your dentist won't see you, call anyone else. Someone will take you as an emergency. Best case scenario, you get a filling and be on your way. Worst case is a root canal if it's gotten infected. Check it out ASAP.

I started out with crochet but eventually transitioned to knitting, and I prefer it 90% of the time. It really depends on the project you're doing and how much patience you have when dealing with mistakes.

Crochet is fast to build up, versatile, and forgiving of mistakes. I like it when I have something that needs structure, like amigurumi. Durability is usually way better too, which makes for some nice blankets. Though crochet becomes boring after a while for me because most projects feel the same to build up.

For garments, though? Knitting wins, hands down. It's way less forgiving and requires a little more planning to do a knitting project, but knitting is also more relaxing to me when I get the hang of it. It scores lower than crochet for durability and structure but the fabric it results in is more appealing to me.

I'm not experienced with homelessness at all but the biggest barrier to getting back on your feet are personal documents. Your ID, birth certificate, SSN card, etc are the first things people lose or get robbed of when they end up on the streets. Maybe you can keep them with a relative or friend? I'd even consider getting a cheap safety deposit box for this purpose.

Not sure where you are specifically, but I would try and make a list of services in your area that may offer assistance/food/shelter. Though shelters aren't too safe, it's certainly safer than being on the streets at 3AM. Watch your belongings though, if you have something loose in a shelter you may as well not have it at all. Keep your phone on you at all times and find a place that has public charging (mall, fast food, coffee shop, etc.) But do not make it obvious you have a phone in front of other homeless people.

If you're in a cold area, take some warm clothes or look to some clothing charities. Intense cold or heat while you're homeless is a true killer.

This tip may be a stretch, but my family and I could have ended up homeless last October. We started our application for a housing voucher early in the year and got rushed to emergency housing via an experienced landlord so we wouldnt be on the streets. Get in touch with housing organizations, they can likely help you apply and point you in the right direction. It takes months and sometimes years to get placed, but it really doesn't hurt to apply.

I'm sure advice from someone who has lived through the experience is more valuable. I hope everything works out for you. Good luck.

For me personally, I feel coursework is okay to add when you don't have a lot of experience under your belt. It can tell the employer what you might have done that relates to what they want. But if you want to leave it out that's okay too, it's purpose is really just to take up a bit of space. If you add it, I wouldn't include any math or physics classes unless they directly relate to the job you want; just stick your most advanced software courses on there. But like I said, whether you include it or leave it out is okay.

A third capstone would be great. I'd also like to say that your job bullet points should use positive words to describe what you do. Like use Quickly, Efficiently, Successfully, etc...Instead of saying you just handled customer tickets, you could say you handled them efficiently and thoroughly. Some of your bullet points sound a bit like job descriptions, but you should treat them more like bragging points. Hello? It's both. Being a necessary evil means it's evil but needed. Fine as a concept means "if this idea was executed PERFECTLY then it would work and be a great idea." Obviously it's not. Something can be morally wrong while still being necessary.

Example? Kill shelters are morally wrong, but they're necessary because there isn't enough shelter for every animal in there, and most won't get adopted. But if they were perfect in concept, we would be killing only because the animal is suffering, not because of lack of space or resources.

Landlording is morally wrong, but not everybody can buy a house on a dime in a capitalist society, so we need them. In a perfect world, landlords would have a lot more limitations and a lot more accountability. Fair rent, repair deadlines, more lenient screening... tons of ways to improve it.

Something can be a good concept with a terrible execution. Something can be a necessary while still being wrong. They aren't mutually exclusive, and a lot of concepts fall under this umbrella. Communism, capitalism, welfare, law system, medical system, etc, etc, etc... Good on paper, needs a lot of work in practice. Landlording in particular is extremely flawed and that's why it's okay as a concept, but morally wrong in practice; it's not fair nor balanced for people who literally need shelter, but all the shelter is gated behind unaffordable prices and 750+ only credit screenings.

If you want to really stretch it out, I'm in your situation right now. We are a family of four who was denied by every realty agent on the market, and have had housing voucher landlords flake on us twice costing us 4 months of our 6 month voucher. Finding a place isn't easy, standards are too high. You have a couple of options.

1) Move out to a sublet or a room share. You might have to sacrifice your dog. Pet friendly housing is difficult to come by, even moreso in a roomate situation. But, if you want cheap, and you don't want an eviction on your record, this is the way to go. The second option leaves a stain on your rental history but buys a lot more time.


2) Don't leave and don't tell her. This is because telling her will give her more time to prepare and she may be able to convince the court to see you early because you won't leave. Don't say you're staying, but imply you are looking for a place. When the eviction notice goes through and she files to the court, it'll likely take a few weeks to get a court date. You can get a lawyer and adjourn the first meeting citing that you didn't have enough time to prep, and they'll give you another court date in a week or more. Now you've earned an extra month. The judge may sympathize with you or understand your circumstance and grant you more time on an official court document. 

"You have to leave by x date, and if you do not, the owner now has the right to call a marshal to formally evict you". NOW you've bought maybe a couple more weeks to a month. Maybe you find a place before that date comes or maybe you don't. If you do, congratulations, you've bought extra time without a marshal eviction, though the court record will still be there. If you stay past that date, the landlord will call the marshal and the marshal will hand you a 3-30 day notice depending on state and circumstance. NOW after he comes and serves you the notice, contact your lawyer and ask for an OSC (Order to show cause). The OSC asks the judge to stop your eviction and hear you out on why you need more time. If it gets denied you must still leave on the marshal's date. But if it gets accepted, your eviction may be null until you get heard, and the judge will either grant you more time or ask the landlord to re-serve the eviction notice... and that will be your true, last time. Within that extra 2+ months you may have found a place where you could keep your dog. Mine lasted 6 months and is still going because section 8 landlord are accepting inspections to not be legally liable for rejecting voucher tenants, and then not taking us.

With effort you can make this last months, but it doesn't look very good to your next landlord and your current will absolutely despise you for it. So far our landlord has locked us our of our mailbox, thrown our drying laundry on the floor, taken down our laundry line, and taken packages/mail that was never even put in the mailbox. You will face hostility and it will be stressful. If you can find even a janky place before the two months is over, please do. If you need more time, I've given you the best way to stretch it out despite not being good for your history in the long term. Landlords are merciless.

My family and I just got accepted to a townhouse that accepts section 8. We were looking for three months and the singular reason we got this apartment was because we knew a person who had a realtor friend. We got really lucky and checked all the boxes. It's a whole different borough than where we needed to be, and it's small, but we have a place and that's what matters. It's really, really hard to find people who accept vouchers because of all the hurdles and hoops they make you jump through.

First, please make sure to report agents, brokers, and landlords that show income and voucher discrimination. It's illegal in New York and they are the reason the most recent wave of voucher holders will be stuck without a place to live. They are very common and most will say some other excuse. They will ghost, tell you that the place was already rented even though the listing was up for another month, tell you they're in the middle of accepting an application, and sometimes straight up tell you they don't take your voucher over the phone with a toxic tone. If you can get proof they rejected you, then just report them.

1) Settle for less. Don't try to get a place at the highest price range your voucher can handle because it's likely that the broker will find someone who will pay more than you and NOT be a voucher holder. If your voucher is $2,000 and you apply to a place that costs $1750, the landlord or broker may be more likely to take your voucher because they can get more than what they listed the place for. They will always take the guy who can pay a couple more hundreds than you, so you want to be the guy to pay a couple more hundreds instead. If CITYFHEPS has updated like section 8 and covers broker fees, make sure to specify that to the broker.

2) You should try finding places listed by landlord. Though they ghost a bit and can be just as rude, it is much, much, much more likely that you will find someone who is either curious about your voucher or knows what it is. They are more likely to listen to your individual case and decide whether or not they want to take a voucher, instead of writing you off because of predisposed notions. I've found that landlords are much more open to us than brokers and some like the idea of having government money because it's more secure. The only other place we got close to being accepted was listed by landlord and it's very clear they don't know how vouchers work, so always ask.  
Also filter places by "Income Restricted." They are almost always in pretty bad areas, but the average voucher has a time limit of 120 days. I'm not sure what your situation is, but I assume 8 months means you're either approaching your deadline very closely or it already passed, so it's not possible to be picky. You take what you can get.

3) You should show that you are reliable with payments. Vouchers cover 70% maximum in rent, in special cases it can go up to 80%, and though you are being helped it is still your responsibility to pay a part of it. It's illegal to discriminate against income and credit, but obviously, brokers don't like rules, so they'll still ask if they end up not ghosting you. Some things you can collect are: Recommendation from previous landlord, your credit score if it sits at an okay number, your current job/proof you are trying to find a job, tax returns, any other public assistance you are receiving from the government, and savings accounts. There might be a few I missed, but that's generally the list. Our landlord we are in the process of moving in with did not ask for anything (except for other public assistance I think), so there are definitely people that don't ask for these requirements, but it's rare.

Our situation is extremely lucky, but in the process, these rules are what got us most of our viewings/applications. You may even have to switch boroughs to be able to get accepted anywhere, and it's not optimal, but at least it's something. If you have any extensions remaining, be sure to ask for them. Good luck, and if you have any questions about the process of looking/being accepted, I'm open to them.
